Your Nightmare Is…

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath
your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what
it would leave behind.
A Nightmare on Elm Street · Since 1984
Elm Street

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

You are the one who is fine during the film and wide awake at two in the morning. Your
own head is where this does its damage.

These films understood exhaustion as a horror engine. The kids on Elm Street do not lose
because they are weak. They lose because they are tired.
You can lock every door in the house. You still have to sleep.
Child's Play · Chucky · Since 1988
Chucky

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the
person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Chucky works precisely because he is absurd. That is the trap: the more accurately you
describe him, the less anybody is going to believe you.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You
know that feeling from real life too.

The franchise is at its best when the adults in the room are the real obstacle, and you
have met those adults.
By the time somebody finally believes you, you will have handled most of it on your own.
Scream · Ghostface · Since 1996
Scream

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost
certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Scream is the only one of these where the killer takes the mask off and turns out to be
somebody who was at the party.

You are the person who calls the twist out loud before it lands. You watch people the
same way you watch films.

The franchise made the rules of horror part of the plot, which means the survivors are
the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.
Everybody is a suspect, including the person who just offered to walk you home.
The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013
The Conjuring

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are

Whatever is here did not come for you. It came for the household, and you are the one
standing in the hallway.

Image via Viking Press

A woman’s maternal instincts can often vanquish even the most formidable foe, and that’s ultimately what happens in King’s scariest animal-centric novel, Cujo. Yet, the days of terrifying torture that the protagonist, Donna Trenton, and her little son, Tad, must endure are almost too much to bear. Cashing in on the terrifying aspects of claustrophobia and feelings of abject helplessness, King crafts a slow-burn masterpiece with this fuzzy look at up-close savagery.

The simple story is about a mom and her child, who, after traveling to a mechanic’s house, become trapped in their car as a once friendly dog tries to claw its way inside and rip them to shreds. The possessed pup, Cujo, is a hulking beast that lunges intermittently at the vehicle, but ultimately seems content to wait them out; it’s blazingly hot outside and his prey will eventually run out of water in the iron prison-tomb of the car. There is another aspect of fear in this book that is one of the most primal that humanity has ever known: fear of the unknown (just ask Lovecraft). To spin it in a slightly different fashion: fear of the unpredictable, and the instability of everyday life. Cujo, while a big boy, starts off the story as a sweet and loving, 200-pound ball of fluff. He playfully chases a rabbit in a hole and is then bit by a rabid bat. Poor Cujo’s quick descension in the fever madness that is rabies is merciless and brutal (the way, sadly, nature can often be). Like many of King’s relentless chimeras, Cujo’s evil side represents addiction; how a passive, and even caring, individual can transform into a feral creature with no regard for anyone other than themselves. Quite the scary concept, indeed. Unlike the Hollywood movie version, King is not concerned with a happy ending, and the tragedy of this tale is frightening on a primordial level.

'Salem’s Lot' (1975)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/salem-s-lot-book-cover-1975.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Doubleday

Mr. King only wrote one novel where vampires are the main focus. That’s all he needed. That novel is, of course, Salem’s Lot, and it certainly is one of the creepiest in his collection. It’s the type of story that steadily builds in its scariness; a growing dread rises in the reader as the inhabitants of Jerusalem’s Lot, a little hamlet in Maine, are taken over, one at a time. King uses such effective imagery here, like claws scratching at foggy windows and undead kids with glowing eyes eerily floating around, that even the most seasoned horror reader is bound to get goosebumps.

The story focuses on a writer, Ben Mears, who returns to his "idyllic" hometown to write a new book about a creepy old house. As the plot progresses, it turns out that the town isn’t that quaint after all, as various secrets ooze out and the sordid details of people’s infidelities, blackmailing, and pilfering are revealed. This is a device to show that this happy little place is morally corrupt and rife to be plundered. Enter some mysterious chaps, Richard Straker (the familiar) and Kurt Barlow (the head vamp) who move into the very house that Ben has always been intrigued (and scared witless) by. The vamps don’t just kill people; they turn them as well, as they seem intent on growing an army of the undead. The vampirism appears to spread like an infection through the populace, a virus that can not be stopped. This creeping sense of doom is daunting enough on its own, but the way that King teases out the attacks, intermittently utilizing subtle, shadowed scares and then extremely gruesome ones, is unsettling to the core. The story culminates in an epic showdown at the house, with Ben and a small cadre of survivors facing off against the bloodthirsty ghouls. This finale is a real nail-biter, terrifying on all fronts. Ben, with the help of a little dude, Mark Petrie, gives the Barlow beast the ole stake through the heart…but this unfortunately doesn’t turn the rest of the townspeople back to normal. It’s this final bit of knowledge that is perhaps the most unsettling of all…

blocks.x: Image via Viking Press

Perhaps, King’s scariest tome is It. The story grew in popularity with the 2-part miniseries that aired in 1990 and then exploded in notoriety with the 2017 film adaptation. However one interprets and enjoys these cinematic works, the general consensus among readers is that they pale in comparison to the haunting, 1,138-page novel. Just about everyone has seen the depiction of the book’s central villain, Pennywise, in either or both of the filmed works, but the sheer manner in which King describes “him” in the book is enough to fuel a thousand nightmares.

The story is about a group of unpopular kids who come together to defeat an eternal evil in their small town of Derry, Maine. It’s split up into two timelines; when they were little ones, and when they come back to Derry, 27 years later (when “it” reemerges). Rather than unravel the sprawling, complicated plot, here are some of the most hair-raising portions of the story. First, there’s the book’s opening, where the little bro, Georgie, of the main character, Bill, is tempted by a “dancing clown” in a storm drain — and then has his arm savagely bitten off by said jester. Then, the female member of the group, Beverly Marsh, hears eerie, echoing voices in her sink drain…and then gets splattered with rancid blood that erupts from therein. Next, the kids (who’ve deemed themselves “The Losers’ Club”) venture to a dilapidated house where they meet Pennywise in the ferocious form of a werewolf, and then a revolting, zombified version of Eddie’s bully brother. Speaking of bullies, the psychotic kid Patrick Hocksetter isn’t spared a horrific death either, as the baby-killer (he murdered his own baby brother) is dealt the hand of being besieged by a bunch of killer leaches. Then, Stan gets stuck in a standpipe, and a bunch of absolutely bone-chilling corpses descend on him, causing permanent psychological damage. And then, there’s the “Deadlights,” the interdimensional location that Pennywise calls his true home; it’s a hellish, rave-like cavernous space of pulsating light, and if one gazes into it, they go permanently insane. There’s just so much haunting imagery in this book, it’s insane, too. Ultimately, the novel is all about abuse, familial neglect, and hidden trauma — which are all scary enough topics on their own, in reality. When merged with the horrific images that King concocts, you’ve got one of the most deviously impactful and scary books of all time.

The Lights Just Went Out
Your Nightmare Is…

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath
your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what
it would leave behind.

A Nightmare on Elm Street · Since 1984

Elm Street

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

You are the one who is fine during the film and wide awake at two in the morning. Your
own head is where this does its damage.

These films understood exhaustion as a horror engine. The kids on Elm Street do not lose
because they are weak. They lose because they are tired.

You can lock every door in the house. You still have to sleep.

Child's Play · Chucky · Since 1988

Chucky

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the
person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Chucky works precisely because he is absurd. That is the trap: the more accurately you
describe him, the less anybody is going to believe you.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You
know that feeling from real life too.

The franchise is at its best when the adults in the room are the real obstacle, and you
have met those adults.

By the time somebody finally believes you, you will have handled most of it on your own.

Scream · Ghostface · Since 1996

Scream

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost
certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Scream is the only one of these where the killer takes the mask off and turns out to be
somebody who was at the party.

You are the person who calls the twist out loud before it lands. You watch people the
same way you watch films.

The franchise made the rules of horror part of the plot, which means the survivors are
the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.

Everybody is a suspect, including the person who just offered to walk you home.

The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013

The Conjuring

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than
personal, which is rarer than it sounds.

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are
the ones who are not alone and refuse to be.

Whatever is here did not come for you. It came for the household, and you are the one
standing in the hallway.

3
'Cujo' (1981)

Image via Viking Press

A woman’s maternal instincts can often vanquish even the most formidable foe, and that’s ultimately what happens in King’s scariest animal-centric novel, Cujo. Yet, the days of terrifying torture that the protagonist, Donna Trenton, and her little son, Tad, must endure are almost too much to bear. Cashing in on the terrifying aspects of claustrophobia and feelings of abject helplessness, King crafts a slow-burn masterpiece with this fuzzy look at up-close savagery.

The simple story is about a mom and her child, who, after traveling to a mechanic’s house, become trapped in their car as a once friendly dog tries to claw its way inside and rip them to shreds. The possessed pup, Cujo, is a hulking beast that lunges intermittently at the vehicle, but ultimately seems content to wait them out; it’s blazingly hot outside and his prey will eventually run out of water in the iron prison-tomb of the car. There is another aspect of fear in this book that is one of the most primal that humanity has ever known: fear of the unknown (just ask Lovecraft). To spin it in a slightly different fashion: fear of the unpredictable, and the instability of everyday life. Cujo, while a big boy, starts off the story as a sweet and loving, 200-pound ball of fluff. He playfully chases a rabbit in a hole and is then bit by a rabid bat. Poor Cujo’s quick descension in the fever madness that is rabies is merciless and brutal (the way, sadly, nature can often be). Like many of King’s relentless chimeras, Cujo’s evil side represents addiction; how a passive, and even caring, individual can transform into a feral creature with no regard for anyone other than themselves. Quite the scary concept, indeed. Unlike the Hollywood movie version, King is not concerned with a happy ending, and the tragedy of this tale is frightening on a primordial level.

2
'Salem’s Lot' (1975)

Image via Doubleday

Mr. King only wrote one novel where vampires are the main focus. That’s all he needed. That novel is, of course, Salem’s Lot, and it certainly is one of the creepiest in his collection. It’s the type of story that steadily builds in its scariness; a growing dread rises in the reader as the inhabitants of Jerusalem’s Lot, a little hamlet in Maine, are taken over, one at a time. King uses such effective imagery here, like claws scratching at foggy windows and undead kids with glowing eyes eerily floating around, that even the most seasoned horror reader is bound to get goosebumps.

The story focuses on a writer, Ben Mears, who returns to his "idyllic" hometown to write a new book about a creepy old house. As the plot progresses, it turns out that the town isn’t that quaint after all, as various secrets ooze out and the sordid details of people’s infidelities, blackmailing, and pilfering are revealed. This is a device to show that this happy little place is morally corrupt and rife to be plundered. Enter some mysterious chaps, Richard Straker (the familiar) and Kurt Barlow (the head vamp) who move into the very house that Ben has always been intrigued (and scared witless) by. The vamps don’t just kill people; they turn them as well, as they seem intent on growing an army of the undead. The vampirism appears to spread like an infection through the populace, a virus that can not be stopped. This creeping sense of doom is daunting enough on its own, but the way that King teases out the attacks, intermittently utilizing subtle, shadowed scares and then extremely gruesome ones, is unsettling to the core. The story culminates in an epic showdown at the house, with Ben and a small cadre of survivors facing off against the bloodthirsty ghouls. This finale is a real nail-biter, terrifying on all fronts. Ben, with the help of a little dude, Mark Petrie, gives the Barlow beast the ole stake through the heart…but this unfortunately doesn’t turn the rest of the townspeople back to normal. It’s this final bit of knowledge that is perhaps the most unsettling of all…

1
'It' (1986)

Image via Viking Press

Perhaps, King’s scariest tome is It. The story grew in popularity with the 2-part miniseries that aired in 1990 and then exploded in notoriety with the 2017 film adaptation. However one interprets and enjoys these cinematic works, the general consensus among readers is that they pale in comparison to the haunting, 1,138-page novel. Just about everyone has seen the depiction of the book’s central villain, Pennywise, in either or both of the filmed works, but the sheer manner in which King describes “him” in the book is enough to fuel a thousand nightmares.

The story is about a group of unpopular kids who come together to defeat an eternal evil in their small town of Derry, Maine. It’s split up into two timelines; when they were little ones, and when they come back to Derry, 27 years later (when “it” reemerges). Rather than unravel the sprawling, complicated plot, here are some of the most hair-raising portions of the story. First, there’s the book’s opening, where the little bro, Georgie, of the main character, Bill, is tempted by a “dancing clown” in a storm drain — and then has his arm savagely bitten off by said jester. Then, the female member of the group, Beverly Marsh, hears eerie, echoing voices in her sink drain…and then gets splattered with rancid blood that erupts from therein. Next, the kids (who’ve deemed themselves “The Losers’ Club”) venture to a dilapidated house where they meet Pennywise in the ferocious form of a werewolf, and then a revolting, zombified version of Eddie’s bully brother. Speaking of bullies, the psychotic kid Patrick Hocksetter isn’t spared a horrific death either, as the baby-killer (he murdered his own baby brother) is dealt the hand of being besieged by a bunch of killer leaches. Then, Stan gets stuck in a standpipe, and a bunch of absolutely bone-chilling corpses descend on him, causing permanent psychological damage. And then, there’s the “Deadlights,” the interdimensional location that Pennywise calls his true home; it’s a hellish, rave-like cavernous space of pulsating light, and if one gazes into it, they go permanently insane. There’s just so much haunting imagery in this book, it’s insane, too. Ultimately, the novel is all about abuse, familial neglect, and hidden trauma — which are all scary enough topics on their own, in reality. When merged with the horrific images that King concocts, you’ve got one of the most deviously impactful and scary books of all time.
